newsitem.title: UK: Zinc prices maintain upward momentum on LME.
newsitem.headline: Zinc prices maintain upward momentum on LME.

text.p: Zinc continued to defy gravity, reaching a fresh seven-year high of $1,600 on Friday, and analysts expect it to continue its rise.
Although the price failed to stay above $1,600, analysts see the next important target $100 higher. "It has got to get through $1,700," said Jim Lennon of Macquarie Bank.
"It could go all the way to $2,000," said Helen Williamson of LME brokers Brandeis, adding that the cash-threes spread could flare out to $200-300, from $50-60 currently.

Chinese producers with big short positions have been caught on the wrong side of the sudden rise, and may have to buy up to 200,000 tonnes of zinc in the market to square their positions, according to Lennon.
Chinese smelters were reported by China Metals magazine to be short by up to 250,000 tonnes of zinc, and since the end of 1996 only 38,000 tonnes of zinc have been put into Singapore warehouses.
"The Chinese producers overestimated how much they could produce and what is of deliverable quality for the LME," Williamson said.

Delays in obtaining further export permits by CNNC, which has already reached its export limits for 1997, may force the Chinese producers to buy around 200,000 tonnes on the market to offset short positions, Lennon said.

Traders said it was uncertain whether the shorts are actually covering in or rolling the positions forward, thereby setting themselves up for a fall in the future. Analysts said that the Chinese were probably using a combination of both, and all eyes were on the crucial September prompt date.
Producers were not able to sell at current levels, since consumers were not willing to buy and some were even destocking.
Consumers were said to be waiting for a downward correction before they buy.

Prices in the second half of 1998 average $1,330, while cash prices are much higher. "There is no opportunity to lock in any reasonable price. Producers can not really capitalise," Lennon said. "It is a classic squeeze," he added.

"It is not that surprising there has been a price rise," said Paul White of the International Lead and Zinc Study Group (ILZSG). He added that sentiment and fundamentals were both good, and Western World consumption is expected to be up 5% this year.
A deficit of 200,000 tonnes is forecast by ILZSG for this year, the same as in 1996.
Others were more sceptical that zinc can maintain its highs, and brokers were nervous of being caught on the wrong side of any sharp downward correction.
"There is a genuine tightness but its not as dramatic as it looks," said a trader. "The price rise was right but it was beyond what most see as sane," he added.
"We would prefer to see a retracement to $1,550," said an analyst, adding that he was "unhappy" with zinc's current movements.
"The zinc bulls have taken the market by the horns," said Angus MacMillan of Billiton Research. "The fundamentals are good but not that good," he added.
